items.title: Games played by Exponential Weights Algorithms
items.summary: arXiv:2407.06676v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the last-iterate convergence properties of the exponential weights algorithm with constant learning rates. We consider a repeated interaction in discrete time, where each player uses an exponential weights algorithm characterized by an initial mixed action and a fixed learning rate, so that the mixed action profile $p^t$ played at stage $t$ follows an homogeneous Markov chain. At first, we show that whenever a strict Nash equilibrium exists, the probability to play a strict Nash equilibrium at the next stage converges almost surely to 0 or 1. Secondly, we show that the limit of $p^t$, whenever it exists, belongs to the set of ``Nash Equilibria with Equalizing Payoffs''. Thirdly, we show that in strong coordination games, where the payoff of a player is positive on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere, $p^t$ converges almost surely to one of the strict Nash equilibria. We conclude with open questions.

items.title: A Survey on Collaborative Mechanisms Between Large and Small Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2505.07460v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) deliver powerful AI capabilities but face deployment challenges due to high resource costs and latency, whereas Small Language Models (SLMs) offer efficiency and deployability at the cost of reduced performance. Collaboration between LLMs and SLMs emerges as a crucial paradigm to synergistically balance these trade-offs, enabling advanced AI applications, especially on resource-constrained edge devices. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of LLM-SLM collaboration, detailing various interaction mechanisms (pipeline, routing, auxiliary, distillation, fusion), key enabling technologies, and diverse application scenarios driven by on-device needs like low latency, privacy, personalization, and offline operation. While highlighting the significant potential for creating more efficient, adaptable, and accessible AI, we also discuss persistent challenges including system overhead, inter-model consistency, robust task allocation, evaluation complexity, and security/privacy concerns. Future directions point towards more intelligent adaptive frameworks, deeper model fusion, and expansion into multimodal and embodied AI, positioning LLM-SLM collaboration as a key driver for the next generation of practical and ubiquitous artificial intelligence.

items.title: MARBLE: An Agentic Benchmark for Spatial Reasoning and Visual Abstraction
items.summary: arXiv:2506.22992v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A central challenge for multimodal language models (MLLMs) in real-world tasks is to abstract visual observations into structured spatial states and reason over how those states change under actions over long horizons. Existing multimodal benchmarks often focus on static question answering, where answers can be directly extracted from images, or assume symbolic states are available and bypass the visual-to-spatial abstraction process. We present MARBLE, a diagnostic benchmark for spatially grounded multimodal reasoning and planning across three agent environments: CUBE, MAZE, and BLOX. MARBLE spans 2D and 3D spatial puzzles under geometric constraints, dynamic layouts, and spatial transformations, with difficulty systematically controlled along two axes: observation format and planning horizon. Extensive evaluations show that frontier MLLMs struggle on MARBLE, with the strongest model GPT-5.4 achieving only a 7.3% average success rate across the three environments in the hardest setting. Pairwise ablations on the open-weight models identify visual-to-spatial abstraction as the major bottleneck: when models must infer spatial states from images instead of receiving human-annotated states, success drops from 50.7% to 3.7% for Gemma-4-31B and from 87.9% to 6.5% for Kimi-K2.6. The results indicate that models often fail to construct precise spatial states from visual observations before planning, a task that is straightforward for humans. Overall, MARBLE reveals the gap in reliable visual-to-spatial abstraction for frontier MLLMs and provides a controlled testbed for measuring progress in spatially grounded multimodal reasoning and planning.

items.title: CXReasonAgent: Evidence-Grounded Diagnostic Reasoning Agent for Chest X-rays

However, large vision-language models (LVLMs) often generate plausible responses that are not faithfully grounded in diagnostic evidence and provide limited visual evidence for verification, while also requiring costly retraining to support new diagnostic tasks, limiting their reliability and adaptability in clinical settings. To address these limitations, we present CXReasonAgent, a diagnostic agent that integrates a large language model (LLM) with clinically grounded diagnostic tools to perform evidence-grounded diagnostic reasoning using image-derived diagnostic and visual evidence. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce CXReasonDail, a multi-turn dialogue benchmark with 1,946 dialogues across 12 diagnostic tasks, and show that CXReasonAgent produces more faithfully grounded responses than LVLMs. These findings highlight the importance of integrating clinically grounded diagnostic tools to enable reliable and verifiable diagnostic reasoning. items.title: Arbor: How Search Policy Shapes Agent Behavior in System Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2606.12563v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Achieving peak performance on modern accelerators requires coordinated optimization across kernels, operator fusion, KV-cache management, quantization, scheduling, and communication overlap, a process that demands weeks of expert effort per model and hardware platform. We present Arbor, a system that gives autonomous agents an explicit optimization tree to reason over, backtrack through, and deepen with experience, with pluggable search policies, scored bandit traversal, parallel agent swarms, and depth-first sweep, sharing a common harness of containerized isolation, automatic rollback, and end-to-end validation. Arbor generalizes across domains: +40% to +193% on six production inference models across two GPU generations, +42.8% on LLM training, and +41% on recommendation training, where agents autonomously wrote kernel-level and framework-level optimizations spanning thousands of lines of code. In controlled ablations where every search policy receives the same agent, tree, and tools, we find that search structure shapes both the magnitude and the nature of the optimizations. The bandit achieves +30.1% through targeted framework fixes, the sweep +26.4% through deep kernel rewrites, and the swarm +33.4% by compounding independent changes. An agent-driven loop that receives the same harness, tools, and information, but selects its own targets reaches +14%, writing 4x more code per percentage point of improvement than Arbor's structured search policies. We additionally introduce an evaluation framework for autonomous loop-based agents spanning efficiency, grounding, robustness, and depth, designed to characterize agent search behavior across long-running optimization campaigns.

items.title: GA-VINO: A Geometry-Aware Variational Physics-informed Neural Operator for Mindlin-Reissner Plates
items.summary: arXiv:2606.16624v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Plate and shell structures are widely used in engineering fields. Rapid response prediction for such structures under complex geometries, heterogeneous materials, and varying loads is important for engineering design, but conventional numerical methods usually require repeated modeling and solution when the physical configuration changes. To address this issue, this study proposes a geometry-aware variational physics-informed neural operator (GA-VINO) for Mindlin-Reissner plates. GA-VINO represents the plate geometry using boundary point clouds and incorporates a material encoder, a load encoder, and a scalar-parameter branch to handle spatially random material fields, spatially varying pressure loads, and sample-level uniform parameters. Through multi-branch point cloud encoding and cross-attention, GA-VINO fuses geometric, material, loading, and query point information, and predicts the transverse deflection and rotations at arbitrary query locations. Unlike conventional data-driven neural operators, GA-VINO requires no labeled solution data during training. Instead, it minimizes a variational physics-informed loss constructed from the discretized total potential energy of the Mindlin-Reissner plate. Compared with grid-based neural operators, GA-VINO directly processes irregular point clouds and allows different physical fields to be discretized on different point sets, avoiding forced interpolation onto a common grid. The method is validated on multiple examples involving different geometries, material fields, and load distributions. The results show that GA-VINO achieves promising accuracy in deflection, rotation, gradient-sensitive, and energy-based metrics, completes full-field inference for new samples within milliseconds, and exhibits promising cross-geometry generalization capability.

items.title: ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity in Agentic Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2607.01919v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic systems enhance their capabilities by invoking external tools and maintaining persistent memory. However, recent tool and memory poisoning attacks can covertly bias agent behavior. We observe that such attacks mounted out of band share a single enabler: each succeeds only by presenting the agent with a contextual state (e.g., tool state and memory) that is not the latest faithfully evolved one. This observation suggests that a continuity check over the contextual state covers this family of attacks. We present ElephantAgent, a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity over the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's context. Before each planning-and-execution cycle, ElephantAgent recomputes the digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest in a linearizable ledger of state transitions, maintained over replicated trusted hardware. The protocol also provides Historical Traceability, a secondary guarantee that keeps state transitions attributable and recoverable. We integrate ElephantAgent into DeepSeek Harness (DSH) and implement ElephantDSH, an agentic system protected by contextual state verification. ElephantDSH withstood all out-of-band attack attempts, from rug pulls and rollbacks to attacks on its own mechanism, and recovered from an in-band prompt injection in all trials. By comparison, existing defenses typically check only what enters the context: of the five we evaluated, all leaked the targeted content under the rollback, and three also under the rug pull. ElephantDSH completed all normal coding tasks with a relative overhead of 1.02-1.07$\times$ over the original DSH with model latency variation removed.

items.title: AgentAbstain: Do LLM Agents Know When Not to Act?
items.summary: arXiv:2607.10059v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agent systems based on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for autonomous tasks, yet existing evaluations mostly focus on task success rather than whether agents know when to abstain. This gap poses real risks: under ambiguity, conflicting constraints, or tool failures, agents may execute unintended and irreversible actions. To close this gap, we present the first systematic evaluation framework for agentic abstention: the calibrated ability of tool-using LLM agents to recognize when not to act. At its core, AgentAbstain is a paired-task benchmark built on an agent-native taxonomy of 8 abstention scenarios across pre-execution reasoning and runtime discovery. It contains 263 paired tasks across 42 executable sandbox environments, where each pair consists of a should-act task and a should-abstain variant produced through a controlled perturbation to the instruction, tool, or environment state. To scale this paired design and resist data contamination, we propose AbstainGen, a fully automated pipeline that synthesizes sandbox environments and generates paired tasks end-to-end, validated by deterministic replay and semantic LLM judges; fresh task instances can be regenerated on demand, and three independent annotators rate 94-98% of sampled tasks as well-designed. Across 17 frontier LLMs in 4 agent harnesses, the best agent (Gemini 3.1 Pro) achieves only 59.5% paired accuracy (correct on both the act and abstain sides of each paired task). More importantly, abstention capability is largely independent of general task-solving capability, indicating that scaling task-solving alone will not close this gap. We further identify failure modes such as post-hoc abstention, in which agents execute irreversible actions before recognizing abstention triggers. Our code and dataset are open-sourced at agentabstain.github.io.

items.title: Disagreement-Guided Agentic Data Curation for Multimodal Safety
items.summary: arXiv:2607.14256v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Written safety policies in multimodal settings define categories whose visual boundaries span many contexts. We study disagreement as a signal for identifying useful synthetic boundary cases. Our pipeline generates policy-conditioned images, selects cases with target--rater or inter-rater disagreement, conditionally escalates unresolved cases, and retrieves the resulting rater-labeled examples as in-context demonstrations. On a failure-enriched multimodal safety benchmark, policy grounding reduces false negative rate (FNR) from 0.875 to 0.413 and raises F1 from 0.220 to 0.731; retrieval from 50 disagreement-selected examples further reduces FNR to 0.245, compared with 0.297 from a 350-example Regular pool. The selected memory also improves a different target-model family, with a smaller gain on a proprietary benchmark with a refined policy. In a blinded human study, experts disagree on 24% of disagreement-guided images and 17% of baseline-curated images. These findings support traceable, disagreement-guided curation for multimodal safety evaluation and example selection.

items.title: Making Mathematical Knowledge Explainable, Accessible and Interoperable Through Large Language Model Integration
items.summary: arXiv:2607.24512v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mathematical models are central to formalizing research problems, yet their documentation often falls short of FAIR principles. Knowledge bases such as the Mathematical Model Database (MathModDB) address this gap by providing curated, semantically rich representations of mathematical models. Built on Wikibase, the same open-source infrastructure underlying Wikidata, MathModDB utilizes Semantic Web technologies to support Linked Open Data, collaborative editing, and the storage of semantically enriched metadata, making it a domain-specific knowledge graph within the broader Wikidata ecosystem. However, access to MathModDB currently requires either navigating a complex web interface or proficiency in SPARQL and Wikibase APIs, posing significant barriers for potential users. In addition, the combination of such curated knowledge bases with actual research data stored, e.g., in Dataverse repository instances, remains a challenge. To overcome these limitations, we propose integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with MathModDB via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that exposes a vector-indexed schema retrieval and Steiner-tree-based join planner, combining dialogue-based natural language interaction with curated, epistemically grounded knowledge. Although instantiated on MathModDB, the architecture can be applied to other Wikibase-based systems. We demonstrate that this approach enables epistemically grounded LLM usage, improves model explainability and accessibility beyond what the standard Wikibase interface offers, and simplifies interoperability with external databases and tools, such as Dataverse data repositories. We illustrate the benefits of combining the accessibility of an LLM with the epistemic safety of a curated knowledge base through the adaptability of the MCP protocol by two use cases.

items.title: CoNav-UAV: Cooperative Dual-Altitude Aerial Navigation via Stackelberg Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2608.01802v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Aerial search missions often require an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to locate a target from only a brief description of its appearance and surroundings, a task known as target-oriented aerial vision-and-language navigation (VLN). The task demands city-scale exploration and grounding as well as collision-free close-range approach, two interleaved processes that are difficult to reconcile within a single agent. Most existing methods adapt the ground VLN paradigm to a single UAV and rely on external assistance to compensate for its inefficiency. A recent attempt deploys two UAVs at complementary altitudes but still depends on privileged sensing and trains the two agents independently, precluding any mutual adaptation. We propose CoNav-UAV, which models the task as a Stackelberg game between a high-altitude leader and a low-altitude follower to capture their sequential decisions and asymmetric observations and utilities, with both agents using only onboard sensing. We introduce Iterative Stackelberg Learning, which tailors optimization to each agent's role: the leader's high-level vision-language reasoning builds on pretrained capabilities and is refined through memory-based in-context learning, while the follower's precise motion control is fine-tuned through DAgger-style expert distillation. Alternating the two updates lets each agent continually adapt to the other's evolving behavior. CoNav-UAV outperforms single- and dual-agent baselines across three high-fidelity urban scenes from the AerialVLN benchmark. It improves success rate by up to 30.8 points on the learning scene and by up to 9.0 points under cross-scene transfer, where the leader reuses its learned memory and the follower is adapted with 2.6-3.7 times less target-scene data. Extensive ablations confirm the contributions of key components and the benefit of mutual adaptation, with consistent gains across VLM backbones.

items.title: JUDOR: CTDE-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for the Co-Optimization of Joint UAV Motion and Decentralized Opportunistic Routing in Delay-Tolerant Network
items.summary: arXiv:2608.04590v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The growing deployment of delay-tolerant networks (DTNs) has made store-carry-forward (SCF) communication indispensable for operating under sparse intermittent connectivity. However, intermittent contact opportunities, finite node buffers, and limited message time-to-live (TTL) degrade message delivery performance and induce network congestion. Yet unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with extended radio coverage and controllable trajectories, can bridge ground-node pairs that would otherwise suffer poor connectivity. Nevertheless, conventional routing schemes decouple UAV motion control from message replication, and consequently fail to leverage UAV mobility to proactively create future contact opportunities. This paper presents JUDOR (Joint-UAV-Decentralized-Opportunistic-Routing), a centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE)-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework optimized for joint discrete UAV heading control and decentralized opportunistic routing. Specifically, we model the tightly coupled UAV motion-routing co-optimization task as a factored partially observable Markov decision process with a shared team reward. JUDOR adopts decentralized actors for local-node execution and a centralized critic used exclusively in training, with optional multi-horizon congestion-hotspot auxiliary supervision. Through evaluation across four distinct traffic modes, JUDOR yields consistent performance gains over both classical and learning-based DTN baselines, including PRoPHET and MaxProp, whilst preserving contact-limited decentralized execution suitable for real-world DTN deployments.

items.title: Beyond Routing Weights: Faithful Response-Level Interpretation of Mixture-of-Experts Reward Models via Contribution Contrast
items.summary: arXiv:2608.06400v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reward models are central to learning from human preferences, yet identifying what drives their predictions remains challenging. Recent sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reward models seek to improve interpretability by routing prompts to specialized experts and characterizing experts through examples with high routing weights. However, routing weights only reveal which prompts an expert $\textit{receives}$, not how it $\textit{judges}$ responses, providing only a partial account of expert behavior. We therefore propose $\textbf{Co}$ntribution-$\textbf{Co}$ntrast ($\textbf{CoCo}$) response-level interpretation, which faithfully characterizes experts' roles using chosen-rejected response pairs with the largest contribution contrasts, jointly capturing routing and preference behavior. Across automatic and human evaluations, CoCo yields more coherent, faithful, and specialized interpretations than router-based, score-based, and sparse autoencoder-based alternatives while maintaining competitive reward modeling accuracy. Overall, we provide a controlled study of how different example-selection signals affect the interpretability of MoE reward models.

items.title: Linearized 2-Simplicial Attention
items.summary: arXiv:2608.09307v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a linearized form of 2-simplicial attention by rewriting the trilinear score as an inner product between a composite query and a key, so that the sum over keys takes the same form as ordinary softmax attention. We then approximate this sum with positive random features and store all previous keys in a fixed-size state, while the sum over second keys stays exact over all previous tokens. This reduces the cost from cubic to quadratic in sequence length, and both keys range over all previous tokens, which windowed 2-simplicial attention does not allow. We implement it with custom Triton kernels and combine it with Kimi Delta Attention to build a model with no softmax attention at all. With 15B equal training tokens on FineWeb-Edu, this model lowers validation loss from 2.35 to 2.32 over a KDA hybrid and lowers LAMBADA perplexity from 40 to 38.

items.title: Meta$^n$: Recursive Self-Improvement through Emergent Depth
items.summary: arXiv:2608.24735v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-improving LLM agents refine answers, not the process that produces those answers. Systems that add a meta-level hold that level fixed, and those that edit themselves must leave part of their own editing machinery untouched to stay stable, capping the meta-depth they realize at roughly two. We present Meta$^n$, which keeps the meta-operation fixed and recurses on its input instead. That operation, $\Omega$, is applied repeatedly to its own products, reading the traces of the solver stack below together with the code that produced them, then writing the next layer as a strategic pre-process and a library of callable helpers. Because $\Omega$ never changes, it cannot destabilize the system, and because its input strictly grows, each layer reasons from a higher vantage than the last. Depth is set by convergence rather than fixed in advance, and an evolutionary archive searches over layer chains. Across two backbones, Meta$^n$ outperforms prior self-improving agents on all eight benchmark families. The sharpest case is ARC-AGI-2, built to resist skill memorization, where it alone scores above zero. Ablations indicate that most of the gain from recursion comes from the conditioning each layer passes to the next, and distinct layer roles emerge with depth although no prompt prescribes them. Code available at https://github.com/minnesotanlp/meta-n

items.title: MAP: A Benchmark on Multimodal Accessibility Planning for Real World Places
items.summary: arXiv:2608.28384v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce MAP, the first benchmark to evaluate multimodal AI systems as assistants for users with accessibility requirements when planning visits to places in the real world. In our evaluation, systems are presented with requests to verify or recommend a point of interest meeting an accessibility requirement. MAP contains two novel assessments: Claim verification for accessibility planning assesses if information on places and stated accessibility features is supported and identifies places that satisfy requested accessibility features. Visual evidence retrieval for accessibility planning checks if a multimodal AI system can select visual evidence for the requested place and accessibility feature. Our methodology supports comparison of AI systems in a setting where place information and accessibility information can change over time by evaluating systems and refreshing ground truth data at scheduled times. The benchmark is based on automatic rating and human rating for a proportion of responses.

items.title: WorkWorlds: Evaluating Agents in a Company Built Before the Task
items.summary: arXiv:2609.23806v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many knowledge work benchmarks are built around single tasks, where the context and files for each task are selected concurrently or after task definition. Research has argued that this construction method does not reflect real workplace work, yet the impact has never been measured under controlled conditions. To compare the two constructions under controlled conditions, we introduce WorkWorlds, an infrastructure that modularizes company components into revision, date, and employee seat to be separately adjusted. Using historical data donated by a real company, we reconstructed a pharmaceutical company, PharmaCo. Two experts with over ten years of industry experience each wrote eight tasks based on real events that occurred at the company, and each independently constructed a task-specific environment for every task. Across 192 controlled evaluations, when the agent was switched from the task-specific environment to all the materials truly visible to the employee, evidence access dropped from 90.4 percent to 72.8 percent, and the criterion pass rate dropped from 76.7 percent to 68.0 percent. However, in cases where the agent found the required evidence, the pass rates under both conditions were almost identical. Furthermore, switching between the environments built by the two experts for the same task resulted in an average pass rate difference of 6.6 percentage points. The three agents also gained by different amounts, which changed the gaps between them. We argue that benchmarks should report how environment materials were selected and, if possible, they should test agent score changes after changing the environment builder.

items.title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy response prediction using pretreatment diffusion and contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging with clinical variables
items.summary: arXiv:2609.26105v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Prediction of pathological complete response before neoadjuvant chemotherapy may facilitate more tailored therapeutic planning for breast cancer patients. This work proposes a deep-learning model for pretreatment data only, combining apparent diffusion coefficient maps, dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging, and clinical variables. The study uses the public ACRIN 6698/I-SPY2 multicenter dataset. The architecture employs EfficientNet-B0 pretrained encoders for image feature extraction and late fusion with clinical information. Multiple clinical variables were evaluated, including age, race, histological type, HR/HER2 subtype, SBR grade, and maximum diameter. Only HR/HER2 subtype improved the average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and was retained in the final model. Using stratified five-fold cross-validation, standalone apparent diffusion coefficient maps achieved a mean AUC of 0.79, whereas dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging achieved 0.74. Adding HR/HER2 subtype improved performance to 0.83 and 0.81, respectively. The final configuration, using both imaging modalities and HR/HER2 subtype, achieved an AUC of 0.86. These results support pretreatment multimodal learning for response prediction, although external validation is required before clinical use.

items.title: Cost-Efficient LLM Evaluation: A Framework for Narrow Confidence Intervals Under Fixed Budgets
items.summary: arXiv:2609.29140v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasingly important role in both academic research and industry. Reliable evaluation helps researchers understand model capabilities and assess progress during model development. However, evaluation can be costly, and researchers often need to assess performance within a fixed budget. Because model outputs can vary across runs, this budget must be allocated between testing different tasks and repeating selected tasks. A confidence interval quantifies the uncertainty in the resulting performance estimate. Obtaining narrower intervals at the same confidence level and evaluation cost provides a more precise assessment of model performance, helping researchers draw clearer conclusions from limited observations. We introduce a framework that allocates a fixed evaluation budget across tasks and repeated runs, with or without full task coverage. The framework then uses disagreements between runs on the same task to bound estimation error, allowing narrower confidence intervals at the same confidence level when the sampled repeats show little variability. When repeated runs on each task yield the same outcome, we prove that our framework achieves the fastest theoretically possible rates for narrowing confidence intervals in the worst case as the number of tasks and the budget for repeats grow. We establish matching lower bounds both when every task must be covered and when tasks may be skipped, even for evaluators who use earlier results to decide which run to carry out next. On LiveCodeBench, our framework yielded narrower confidence intervals on average than uniform random sampling in 15 of 16 model configurations, with a median width reduction of 30.6% at the same confidence level and the same budget of 1,100 outputs per configuration.

items.title: MemeLogos: Knowledge-Driven Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning for Harmful Meme Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2610.15463v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: With the rapid proliferation of social media, harmful memes have become a growing threat to online ecosystems. Their harmfulness is often implicitly conveyed through complex interactions among visual, textual, and contextual cues, making accurate detection challenging. Recent studies have introduced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and external knowledge into harmful meme detection. However, existing methods mainly retrieve similar instances or auxiliary information, limiting their ability to capture reusable harmfulness knowledge and underlying reasoning mechanisms, and thus constraining both detection performance and interpretability. To address these challenges, we propose MemeLogos, a knowledge-driven retrieval-augmented reasoning framework for harmful meme detection. MemeLogos abstracts recurring harmfulness patterns and reasoning structures from diverse harmful cases into reusable knowledge units and organizes them into a dedicated star-shaped knowledge graph. By combining structured knowledge retrieval with an explicit multi-stage reasoning process inspired by cognitive mechanisms, MemeLogos leverages retrieved knowledge to guide harmfulness reasoning, improving both detection reliability and interpretability. Extensive experiments show that MemeLogos consistently outperforms existing harmful meme detection methods while generating more coherent and interpretable reasoning, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured harmfulness knowledge for multimodal content understanding.

items.title: Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25096v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona-driven simulations. Its questions are constructed by linking entities and intermediate answers across heterogeneous sources, requiring agents to identify the relevant sources, carry evidence between them, and produce a grounded answer. To systematically evaluate LLMs on these retail workflows, we develop RetailRAG, a retail-aware framework equipped with auto-schema briefing, source-routed plan chaining, and diagnostic plan revision. RetailRAG consistently outperforms existing agentic RAG baselines across all evaluation axes, serving as a strong reference system for assessing LLM agents on retail workflows. On RetailBridge, evaluating ten LLM backbones with RetailRAG reveals multi-source chaining as the dominant bottleneck across providers and model scales, suggesting that reliable retail agents require explicit cross-source orchestration rather than scaling alone. items.title: DataPraxis: Scaling Analytics Tasks via Verified Workspace Evolution
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26924v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: General-purpose agents are increasingly expected to perform professional analytics work, which requires sustained reasoning, iterative investigation, and reliable evidence. Training these capabilities requires diverse and challenging tasks. However, generating tasks directly from raw data often overlooks deeper questions that emerge through analysis and provides limited evidence for verification. To address these limitations, we introduce DataPraxis, an analytics task synthesis framework based on verified workspace evolution. The framework progressively enriches workspaces with validated findings and artifacts, then inherits and combines these workspaces to uncover deeper questions. It constructs tasks from accumulated findings and their dependencies, verifying analytical results both during evolution and after task assembly. Using this framework, we construct DataPraxis-5K, a dataset of 5,000 verified trajectories spanning diverse domains and output formats, to train DataPraxis-27B and DataPraxis-35B-A3B. DataPraxis-27B achieves 55.11 on DABStep and 51.9 on JobBench, matching or surpassing frontier models such as GLM-5.2. items.title: DuoCook: An Overcooked-Inspired Benchmark for Visual Planning and Coordination
items.summary: arXiv:2610.31511v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget. We introduce an Overcooked-inspired benchmark for evaluating these capabilities in Unreal Engine environments constructed using coding agents. A single vision-language model controls both players from top-down visual observations \rev{through separate per-player decision calls}, selecting high-level actions \rev{and image-labeled target cells} while the engine executes navigation. The benchmark contains 20 maps in five categories. These categories support evaluation of \rev{two-player} coordination under equipment contention, changing terrain, and handoff dependencies. A prop legend and pot ingredient-count indicators provide explicit visual cues, while grid-based destinations support spatial grounding\rev{; text gives no station coordinates, so target locations come mainly from the image}. The evaluation compares \rev{five VLMs and a privileged scripted reference policy on all 20 maps}, measuring task score, order completion, delivery precision, \rev{aim accuracy}, and model API expenditure. \rev{Two paired ablations on all 20 maps toggle a shared self-authored notebook and reduce the textual prompt from about 3,600 to about 440 words while keeping the images fixed.} \rev{The strongest model completes 35\% of orders and exceeds the scripted reference, which has ground-truth station access; the notebook's effect is mixed in sign and not statistically reliable, and reducing the prompt text lowers the score of two models while leaving the other three nearly unchanged.} Together, the environment design and evaluation protocol provide a framework for investigating how visual state tracking and task scheduling contribute to coordinated cooking behavior.

items.title: Query-Driven Learning for Lifted Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34747v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning and reasoning are both essential to intelligent agents, but have traditionally been treated as two separate stages: first learning a knowledge base from data (or taking one as given), and then verifying queries as if the knowledge base were complete. This separation has been shown to be inefficient when the downstream goal is to verify only a small set of queries. Moreover, it neglects the possibility that data and a knowledge base contain partial yet complementary information, requiring an agent to combine both sources to justify or refute a query. Motivated by the need to integrate learning and reasoning more tightly, we study the problem of query-driven learning for reasoning. More specifically, we extend prior work to the first-order setting, which is critical for practical applications as the number of ground atoms typically grows rapidly. We begin by asking when validating or refuting a universal query given partial data and knowledge base is even possible, and identify a necessary and sufficient condition called bounded concealment. We then propose a quasi-polynomial-time algorithm that solves the task at the lifted level. Finally, we establish soundness and completeness guarantees relative to space-bounded lifted proofs, along with quasipolynomial sample and runtime bounds, demonstrating that lifted query-driven reasoning can be efficient even when unrestricted knowledge-base learning is not.

items.title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery from Clinical Data
items.summary: arXiv:2611.08922v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes from multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive capability. More broadly, these findings suggest that foundation model features revealed through interpretability methods could expand clinical understanding of disease. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph.

items.title: Learning When to Think: Dual-Reference Offline Optimization for Adaptive VLM Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09154v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reasoning traces improve vision-language models on complex multimodal tasks, but forcing every input to follow a long reasoning process leads to overthinking and unnecessary inference cost. We study adaptive fast/slow thinking for VLMs, where one model answers directly for simple inputs and reasons step by step when needed. Fast answers and slow traces often come from distinct behavior policies, making a single-reference offline objective misweight one mode. We propose DUAL-REFERENCE BOLT (DR-BOLT), which distinguishes the desired fast/slow mixture reference from the sampling distribution and corrects their mismatch in reward-weighted training. Fast/slow partition competition explains routing in the optimal target; an efficient source-wise correction approximates the exact objective when response formats are well separated. Matched Qwen3-VL comparisons use identical candidate banks to isolate the objective from slow-teacher quality. DR-BOLT improves score-length trade-offs over the evaluated offline and online baselines on ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, with a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and a 2.90-fold end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO. These results support adaptive reasoning in the studied two-reference setting, while broader robustness remains open. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongbinLin3589/DR-BOLT.

items.title: Measuring and Attributing Evidence Sensitivity in Medical Vision-Language Models via Symmetric Counterfactual Controls
items.summary: arXiv:2611.13006v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) asked closed clinical questions ("Is there a polyp?") can score well by relying on the question rather than the image, and current hallucination benchmarks cannot separate true visual discrimination from editing shortcuts or shifts in the answer threshold. We introduce a Counterfactual Evidence Framework that pairs each lesion erasure with a shape- and tool-matched control edit elsewhere in the image, adds same-site ring controls, restored and partial erasures, degraded views and natural negatives, tests on held-out inpainting tools, separates discrimination (the Evidence Sensitivity Gap, ESG, and AUROC) from the answer threshold, and checks the labels with blinded physician readers and hidden-state probes. Across 507 main-test cases (1,115 views), nine frontier VLMs claim 41.1% to 61.6% of erased lesions (ESG 0.269 to 0.470), whereas MedScope-4B, a Qwen3.5-4B agent trained on automatically built counterfactual trajectories, claims 9.6% (ESG 0.758; p <= 0.001 in all 27 primary comparisons). Physician readers support automated erasure in colonoscopy, where frontier models still claim 45% of erased lesions against 1% for MedScope-4B, but call a finding present on 54.7% of pooled erased reads across all sources, which bounds what unverified erasure can certify. Across 12 pre-registered training or system arms and 270 decision policies screened under a rule fixed in advance, every apparent utility gain comes from shifting the threshold rather than improving held-out discrimination, and probes point to perception as the remaining limit. We also report a 0/48 pneumothorax failure on an external cohort; retraining with pneumothorax patients in every stage finds 53% of pneumothoraxes on new patients without changing the main-test results.

items.title: GenPFN: An In-Context Tabular Foundation Model Approach for Augmenting Small Datasets in Engineering
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14804v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Costly simulations and experiments limit the data available for engineering design. This paper proposes GenPFN, a training-free candidate generator guided by a pretrained tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) classifier with fixed weights. The context contains evaluated designs labeled desired (Class 1) or undesired (Class 0). GenPFN interpolates between desired designs and refines candidates using gated classifier gradients and Gaussian noise. Each candidate is evaluated using the problem's constraints and objective functions. Evaluated desired designs and their objective values augment the context for regression training. Evaluation spans fourteen selected problems, including a two-parameter benchmark and a 44-parameter hull problem. In paired comparisons, GenPFN with TabPFN v1 achieves higher class satisfaction and lower realism distance than the tested adversarial, variational-autoencoder and diffusion generators. The variational-autoencoder generator provides greater coverage and diversity. Relative to the synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE), GenPFN provides lower coverage distance and greater diversity. Among observed paired regression fits, augmentation reduces estimated AutoGluon validation mean squared error by 62.1% relative to context-only training. A hull-stern case study yields 99.3% propeller-compatible candidates versus 1.4% among randomly sampled context designs. Generation followed by evaluation produces sample sets that augment limited datasets and support training more accurate predictive models.

items.title: Agentic On-Policy Distillation Implicitly Reshapes LLMs' ReAct Patterns
items.summary: arXiv:2611.19244v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers specialized capabilities to language-model agents, but its cross-domain effects on interaction remain unclear. We investigate how OPD reshapes ReAct interaction patterns across mathematics, ALFWorld, and $\tau^2$-bench, focusing on reasoning, actions, and observation acquisition. General-reasoning supervision reduces mathematical tool attempts from 70.4% to 14.4% while increasing accuracy from 16.7% to 38.0%; code-interpreter supervision improves household actions and retail queries. In contrast, ALFWorld supervision reduces $\tau^2$-bench accuracy from 41.5% to 6.6%, accompanied by frequent tool calls that violate user-information dependencies. To address negative transfer using only source-domain training trajectories, we explore selective OPD guided by teacher preference changes before and after domain-specific RL. Retaining the top 95% of positions raises $\tau^2$ accuracy from 11.5% to 29.9% with a source-learning trade-off.

items.title: I2I Backdoor: Backdoor Attacks against Image-to-Image Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2407.10445v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: With the rapid development of deep learning technology, deep learning-based Image-to-Image (I2I) networks have become the predominant choice for I2I tasks like image super-resolution and denoising. Despite their remarkable performance, the security of I2I networks has not been thoroughly investigated. While some studies have probed their susceptibility to adversarial attacks, none have explored the backdoor attack against I2I networks, which is a more stealthy and severe threat. In this work, for the first time, we comprehensively investigate the vulnerability of I2I networks to backdoor attacks. We propose a backdoor attack against I2I tasks, where the backdoored I2I network behaves normally on clean input images, yet outputs a specific inappropriate image when the backdoor trigger appears on the input image. To achieve such an I2I backdoor attack, we design a universal adversarial perturbation (UAP) generation algorithm for I2I networks, where the generated UAP is used as the trigger for the I2I backdoor. Besides, multi-task learning (MTL) with dynamic weighting methods is employed in the backdoor training process to gain better results. Expanding our focus beyond I2I tasks, we extend our I2I backdoor to attack downstream tasks, including image classification and object detection. Specifically, the backdoor-triggered image processed by the backdoored image denoising network can fool the downstream image classifiers and object detectors. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the I2I backdoor on state-of-the-art I2I network architectures as well as the robustness against different backdoor defenses.

items.title: MultiAgentBench: Evaluating the Collaboration and Competition of LLM agents
items.summary: arXiv:2503.01935v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities as autonomous agents, yet existing benchmarks either focus on single-agent tasks or are confined to narrow domains, failing to capture the dynamics of multi-agent coordination and competition. In this paper, we introduce MultiAgentBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate LLM-based multi-agent systems across diverse, interactive scenarios. Our framework measures not only task completion but also the quality of collaboration and competition using novel, milestone-based key performance indicators. Moreover, we evaluate various coordination protocols (including star, chain, tree, and graph topologies) and innovative strategies such as group discussion and cognitive planning. Notably, gpt-4o-mini reaches the average highest task score, graph structure performs the best among coordination protocols in the research scenario, and cognitive planning improves milestone achievement rates by 3%. Code and datasets are public available at https://github.com/MultiagentBench/MARBLE.

items.title: FedS2R: One-Shot Federated Domain Generalization for Synthetic-to-Real Semantic Segmentation in Autonomous Driving
items.summary: arXiv:2507.19881v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Federated domain generalization has shown promising progress in image classification by enabling collaborative training across multiple clients without sharing raw data. However, its potential in the semantic segmentation of autonomous driving remains underexplored. In this paper, we propose FedS2R, the first one-shot federated domain generalization framework for synthetic-to-real semantic segmentation in autonomous driving. FedS2R comprises two components: an inconsistency-driven data augmentation strategy that generates images for unstable classes, and a multi-client knowledge distillation scheme with feature fusion that distills a global model from multiple client models. Experiments on five real-world datasets, Cityscapes, BDD100K, Mapillary, IDD, and ACDC, show that the global model significantly outperforms individual client models and is only 2 mIoU points behind the model trained with simultaneous access to all client data. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of FedS2R in synthetic-to-real semantic segmentation for autonomous driving under federated learning

items.title: How K-12 Teachers Adapt Generative AI to Local Classroom Demands: Cultural Distance Between GenAI Defaults and Everyday Teaching Practices
items.summary: arXiv:2509.10780v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is entering K-12 classrooms, but its default culture does not always fit local teaching. Existing accounts either treat this misfit as macro-level structural bias or examine it through single-case studies; neither captures how much work teachers must do to make outputs usable across tasks. This exploratory, theory-building qualitative study introduces cultural distance, the gap between GenAI's default cultural repertoire and the situated demands of teachers' practice. Through interviews with 30 K-12 teachers who frequently use GenAI, 10 each from South Africa, Taiwan, and the United States, we identified three levels defined by the effort teachers invested and whether it yielded a usable output: low (minor edits), mid (sustained prompting and revision), and high (structural gaps rooted in unsupported languages, undigitized knowledge, or policy filters that no teacher effort can close). We present cultural distance as a promising framework requiring further examination and draw implications for designers, policymakers, and educators.

items.title: Improving Outdoor Multi-cell Fingerprinting-based Positioning via Mobile Data Augmentation
items.summary: arXiv:2509.19405v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate outdoor positioning in cellular networks is hindered by sparse, heterogeneous measurement collections and the high cost of exhaustive site surveys. This paper introduces a lightweight, modular mobile data augmentation framework designed to enhance multi-cell fingerprinting-based positioning using operator-collected minimization of drive test (MDT) records. The proposed approach decouples spatial and radio-feature synthesis: kernel density estimation (KDE) models the empirical spatial distribution to generate geographically coherent synthetic locations, while a 1-nearest-neighbor (1NN)-based block produces augmented per-cell radio fingerprints. The architecture is intentionally training-free, interpretable, and suitable for distributed or on-premise operator deployments, supporting privacy-aware workflows. We both validate each augmentation module independently and assess its end-to-end impact on fingerprinting-based positioning using a real-world MDT dataset provided by an Italian mobile network operator across diverse urban and peri-urban scenarios. Results show that the proposed KDE-1NN augmentation consistently improves positioning performance with respect to state-of-the-art approaches, reducing the median positioning error by up to 30% (specifically achieved at an augmentation rate of x30 in the highly sparse highway scenario). We also observe region-dependent saturation effects, which emerge most rapidly in scenarios with high user density where the information gain from additional synthetic samples quickly diminishes. Overall, the framework offers a practical, low-complexity path to enhance operator positioning services using existing mobile data traces.

items.title: MonitorVLM:A Vision Language Framework for Safety Violation Detection in Mining Operations
items.summary: arXiv:2510.03666v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Industrial accidents, particularly in high-risk domains such as surface and underground mining, are frequently caused by unsafe worker behaviors. Traditional manual inspection remains labor-intensive, error-prone, and insufficient for large-scale, dynamic environments, highlighting the urgent need for intelligent and automated safety monitoring. In this paper, we present MonitorVLM, a novel vision--language framework designed to detect safety violations directly from surveillance video streams. MonitorVLM introduces three key innovations: (1) a domain-specific violation dataset comprising 9,000 vision--question--answer (VQA) samples across 40 high-frequency mining regulations, enriched with augmentation and auxiliary detection cues; (2) a clause filter (CF) module that dynamically selects the Top-$K$ most relevant clauses, reducing inference latency by 13.56% while maintaining accuracy; and (3) a behavior magnifier (BM) module that enhances worker regions to improve fine-grained action recognition, yielding additional gains of 3.45% in precision and 8.62% in recall. Experimental results demonstrate that MonitorVLM significantly outperforms baseline vision--language models, achieving improvements of 22.01% in precision, 34.22\% in recall, and 28.37% in F1 score over the 72B unfine-tuned baseline. A lightweight web-based interface further integrates MonitorVLM into practical workflows, enabling automatic violation reporting with video timestamping. This study highlights the potential of multimodal large models to enhance occupational safety monitoring in mining and beyond.

items.title: Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
items.summary: arXiv:2601.16823v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities, yet it remains unclear to what extent these reflect sophisticated recall or genuine reasoning ability. We introduce chess as a controlled testbed aimed at disentangling these faculties. Leveraging the game's structure and scalable engine evaluations, we construct a taxonomy of positions varying in density of relevant priors -- ranging from common states solvable by memorization to completely novel ones requiring generalization. Crucially, our approach achieves this distinction without requiring explicit knowledge of the models' training data. Applying this taxonomy, we combine a longitudinal analysis of the GPT lineage with a rigorous evaluation of contemporary models, including Claude Opus and Gemini. Our analysis reveals a steep gradient: performance consistently degrades as the density of relevant priors decreases. Notably, for tasks with few relevant priors, base model performance regresses to the random-play baseline, and all models propose illegal moves at sharply increasing rates, indicating that they fail to reliably apply the fixed rules of the game in unfamiliar positions. While newer models improve, progress slows significantly for tasks with sparse priors. Furthermore, while reasoning-augmented inference improves performance, its relative marginal benefit per token decreases in the absence of relevant priors. These results suggest limitations in systematic generalization, highlighting the need for mechanisms beyond scale to achieve robust performance when deprived of relevant priors.

items.title: PANC: Prior-Aware Normalized Cut for Training-Free In-Context Segmentation
items.summary: arXiv:2602.06912v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study training-free in-context segmentation with externally annotated context priors: given a target image and a small set of foreground/background tokens extracted from annotated context images, the goal is to segment the corresponding target concept without training, fine-tuning, or target-image clicks. Existing ViT-token spectral methods such as TokenCut are class-agnostic and can select the wrong object in multi-object scenes, or become unstable in low-semantic texture-dominated domains. We propose PANC, a prior-aware spectral segmentation pipeline that injects external labeled tokens into a frozen ViT affinity graph through two foreground/background anchor nodes. The anchors do not clamp target-image tokens; instead, they softly bias the Normalized Cut eigenspace while preserving the target-image affinity structure. PANC further uses prior-aware sign stabilization and prior-driven thresholding to obtain deterministic masks. Across heterogeneous saliency datasets and homogeneous low-semantic domains, PANC improves over architecture-matched no-prior token-graph baselines, with the largest gains in settings where class-agnostic saliency is ambiguous or weak.

items.title: Generating Adversarial Events: A Motion-Aware Point Cloud Framework
items.summary: arXiv:2602.08230v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Event cameras have been widely adopted in safety-critical domains such as autonomous driving, robotics, and human-computer interaction. A pressing challenge arises from the vulnerability of deep neural networks to adversarial examples, which poses a significant threat to the reliability of event-based systems. Nevertheless, research into adversarial attacks on events is scarce. This is primarily due to the non-differentiable nature of mainstream event representations, which hinders the extension of gradient-based attack methods. In this paper, we propose MA-ADV, a novel \textbf{M}otion-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{Adv}ersarial framework. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to generate adversarial events by leveraging point cloud representations. MA-ADV accounts for high-frequency noise in events and employs a diffusion-based approach to smooth perturbations, while fully leveraging the spatial and temporal relationships among events. Finally, MA-ADV identifies the minimal-cost perturbation through a combination of sample-wise Adam optimization, iterative refinement, and binary search. Extensive experimental results validate that MA-ADV ensures a 100\% attack success rate with minimal perturbation cost, and also demonstrate enhanced robustness against defenses, underscoring the critical security challenges facing future event-based perception systems.

items.title: Colosseum: Auditing Collusion in Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2602.15198v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent systems, where LLM agents communicate through free-form language, enable sophisticated coordination for solving complex cooperative tasks. This surfaces a unique safety problem when a group of agents forms a coalition and colludes to pursue secondary goals and degrade the joint objective. In this paper, we present Colosseum, a framework for auditing LLM agents' collusive behavior in multi-agent settings. We ground how agents cooperate through a formal multi-agent decision-making framework and measure action-based collusive behavior in actions via regret relative to the cooperative optimum and compare it with communication-based collusive behavior. Colosseum enables audits of LLM agents for collusion under benign settings, different coalition objectives, persuasion tactics, and network topologies. We then introduce a new behavioral probe by creating secret communication channels between agents, showing that most out-of-the-box models exhibit a propensity to collude under this probe, which we term emergent collusion. Furthermore, we discover ``collusion on paper'' when agents plan to collude in text but often pick non-collusive actions. Colosseum provides a new way to audit collusion in cooperative multi-agent systems while presenting observations about how collusion emerges, what affects collusion efficacy, and which strategies may mitigate it.

items.title: PEARL: Personalized Streaming Video Understanding with Runtime-Defined Concepts
items.summary: arXiv:2603.20422v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unlike humans, who learn new concepts from a continuous visual stream, existing personalized vision-language models (VLMs) internalize a predefined concept set during training and operate on static images or offline videos. They cannot register a concept that a user defines in the middle of a stream, nor recall the earlier moments in which it appeared. We formalize this task as Personalized Streaming Video Understanding (PSVU) and introduce PSVU-Bench, the first benchmark for this task, which annotates 132 videos with timestamped questions. Its Concept-Definition, Real-Time and Past-Time QA ask a model to register concepts at arbitrary timestamps, recognize their current state, including user-defined actions, and retrieve their historical evidence. We propose PEARL, a strong plug-and-play baseline that stores user-defined concepts apart from archived video clips and rewrites each query with concept descriptions to retrieve the relevant history. Grounding a named concept in video is a skill shared by all concepts. We therefore construct PSVU-10K, a training set of verified concept questions on public internet videos, and train the retriever and answering VLM of PEARL on it once. Concepts defined at test time still require no training. Applied to three architectures without training, PEARL improves Real-Time QA by 15.05% and Past-Time QA by 12.60% on average over the corresponding offline models, and all three surpass existing online video models on both QA types. Training further improves PEARL on Qwen3-VL-8B by 8.66% on Real-Time QA and 9.39% on Past-Time QA, with gains in every category. items.title: WorldComposer: Generative High-Fidelity Simulation with Digital Cousins for Generalizable Robot Learning and Evaluation
items.summary: arXiv:2604.15805v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning robust robot policies in real-world environments requires diverse data augmentation, yet scaling real-world data collection is costly due to the need for acquiring physical assets and reconfiguring environments. Therefore, augmenting real-world scenes into simulation has become a practical augmentation for efficient learning and evaluation. We present WorldComposer, an automated generative Real2Sim2Real framework that maps real-world panoramas into high-fidelity, task-ready simulation environments and further synthesizes diverse Digital Cousins through scene and object variations. Combined with high-quality physics engines and realistic assets, WorldComposer supports interactive manipulation across rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Additionally, we incorporate multi-room stitching to construct consistent large-scale environments for long-horizon tasks. Experiments demonstrate a strong sim-to-real correlation validating our platform's fidelity, and show that extensively scaling up data generation leads to significantly better generalization to unseen scene and object variations, demonstrating the effectiveness of Digital Cousins for generalizable robot learning and evaluation.

items.title: HorizonBench: Long-Horizon Personalization with Evolving Preferences
items.summary: arXiv:2604.17283v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Personal assistants now talk with the same user for months, and users' preferences change as their lives change; an assistant that keeps serving a preference the user has outgrown fails that user. Real conversations do not record when or why a preference changed, and existing benchmarks either hold preferences fixed or have the user state the change, so they cannot tell whether a model forgot what the user said or failed to update its belief about the user. We introduce HorizonBench and its data generator, which samples how a user's preferences change and generates six months of conversation from that sequence; each change follows a life event that the user mentions without stating the new preference. A human longitudinal preference dataset that we collect and release, 83,024 ratings from 160 people over 13 weeks, sets how often and how much life events change preferences. HorizonBench contains 4,245 questions from 360 users, and when a preference has changed, its earlier value is one of the answer options. All 25 frontier models we evaluate choose the outdated preference more often than evenly spread errors would predict, and the best reaches 52.8% accuracy. Two of the newest models score no higher when given only the relevant conversations than with the full history, yet one added sentence stating the change raises their accuracy by 11 to 22 points, and retrieval and memory methods do not recover the lost accuracy. Remembering what a user said and knowing what the user prefers now are therefore separate capabilities, and HorizonBench, its generator, and the human dataset support research on both.

items.title: MedExAgent: Training LLM Agents to Ask, Examine, and Diagnose in Noisy Clinical Environments
items.summary: arXiv:2605.07058v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Real-world clinical diagnosis is a complex process in which the doctor is required to obtain information from both interaction with the patient and conducting medical exams. Additionally, the doctor needs to adapt to different patient personas, as well as noisy and incomplete information that can happen at any time during the process. However, existing benchmarks for medical LLMs and methods for automatic diagnosis largely simplify this process by reducing it to single-turn question answering, noise-free conversations, or sequential exam making, etc., ignoring the interactive and uncertain nature of clinical diagnosis. In this paper, we aim to address this gap by formalizing clinical diagnosis as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) with three action types: questioning the patient, ordering medical exams as tool calls, and issuing a diagnosis. We also introduce a systematic noise model comprising seven patient noise types and three exam noise types. Using our proposed environment, we train an effective diagnosis agent, \textbf{MedExAgent}, through a two-stage pipeline that first performs supervised finetuning on synthetic conversations structured after the Calgary-Cambridge model for clinical interviews, and then applies DAPO to optimize a composite reward capturing diagnostic accuracy, tool call quality, and exam cost including financial cost and patient discomfort. Through extensive experiments and ablation studies, we demonstrate that MedExAgent achieves diagnostic performance comparable to larger models while maintaining cost-efficient examination strategies.

items.title: LLM-Assisted Reranking to Operationalize Nuanced Objectives in Recommender Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2606.02883v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recommender systems shape what information we see, raising concerns about filter bubbles, radicalization, polarization, and social inequality. Large language models (LLMs) enable more powerful personalization that may intensify these dynamics, yet most recommenders are tuned for engagement or narrow accuracy metrics, with little attention to broader social effects. We investigate whether LLM-assisted reranking, while improving personalization, inadvertently amplifies exposure to ideologically congenial, extreme, or conspiratorial political content, a risk theorized but not yet empirically characterized. Using real YouTube trajectories, we rerank the platform's sidebar candidates by zero-shot prompting across three models, alongside an embedding baseline, and evaluate relevance, ideological alignment and diversity, and exposure to conspiratorial or extremist content. We find that (i) under a pure personalization instruction, reranking improves relevance while narrowing ideological exposure and, on two of three models, promoting problematic content for users with such histories; the third model, which declines most explicitly partisan requests, points to model-specific guardrails; (ii) lightweight prompt-level constraints substantially reduce problematic exposure on all three models, while the regularized rerankers still rank above the platform baseline on relevance; and (iii) synthetic experiments varying topical and partisan cues independently show no fixed preference between them: topic dominates on abortion and immigration, while partisanship takes over on elections, where the topical signal is weaker. Our results highlight the power of LLMs to operationalize contextual nuance in high-stakes political recommendation, and underscore the need to evaluate LLM-assisted personalization beyond accuracy and to treat prompt design as a value-laden choice rather than a neutral default.

items.title: Accounting for Purchased Artificial Intelligence Inference in Corporate Greenhouse Gas Inventories: A Token-Based Method
items.summary: arXiv:2606.10660v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Purchased artificial intelligence (AI) inference belongs in Scope 3 Category 1 of a corporate greenhouse gas inventory, yet practice omits it or applies a spend-based factor that gives 1.7 to 12.3 times the physical estimate and cannot tell one model or region from another. This paper sets out a token-based method and open dataset: a cradle-to-gate boundary, four tiers of activity data, an effective-token basis, a four-term factor (serving electricity, embodied hardware, data-centre construction, disclosed final training runs) and a rule resolving any model identifier and region to a factor. Inference footprints span twelve times between model classes and nine between regions. The mid-class factor, 0.039 kg of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) per million billed tokens at the world-average grid, is the low end of a stated structural range: a less efficient serving configuration raises it 2.8 times, and replacing the training term with all model development, on its own boundary, gives 1.5 to 2.9 times it. Input bands alone give -18% to +29%. Published per-query energy estimates that can describe a mid-class model are 2.4 to 7.2 times the mid-class energy, above its structural range in four of five rows; those that can describe a frontier-class model bracket it at 0.7 to 1.6 times. Worked examples give 8.5 kg CO2e a year for a 200-person firm, and 2.1 tonnes for fifty developers using agentic coding tools on a mid-class model or 8.3 tonnes on a frontier-class one. items.title: Multi-Modal Environment-Aware Beam Management for Massive MIMO: A Geometry-Driven Virtual Base Station Framework
items.summary: arXiv:2606.26567v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-frequency massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems promise ultra-high data rates. However, efficient beam management remains challenging due to the prohibitive beam training overhead and intricate coordination required in multi-user MIMO (MU-MIMO) scenarios. To address these bottlenecks, environment-aware communications have emerged as a promising paradigm, leveraging site-specific knowledge to circumvent exhaustive pilot-based beam training and streamline multi-user communications. In this paper, we propose a geometry-driven framework that utilizes multi-modal environmental data, specifically regional 3D light detection and ranging (LiDAR) point clouds and location information, to construct an offline virtual base station (VBS) database. By modeling dominant reflection paths via mirror symmetry across building facades reconstructed from the point clouds, the VBS database provides a compact and sparse description of the wireless propagation environment. Given a user location, the VBS representation supports online coarse channel reconstruction and the generation of a beamspace prior. To refine the coarse estimates, we design a VBS-assisted orthogonal-pilot (VOP)-based partial beam training scheme with limited online measurements. Finally, to coordinate beam selection under inter-user interference, we develop a hierarchical dual-agent dueling double deep Q-network for coordinated beam selection (DD3QN-CBS). Simulation results show that the proposed framework improves effective spectral efficiency over the evaluated stochastic, heuristic, and conventional learning-based baselines, while achieving competitive performance with fewer online beam measurements.

items.title: Brownian Bridge Diffusion-Assisted Joint Channel Estimation and Data Detection for Jamming-Resilient OFDM Receivers
items.summary: arXiv:2606.28778v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In next-generation wireless networks, the growing density of devices and limited spectrum resources pose severe jamming challenges to fragile legitimate communication links in the wireless electromagnetic environment. Crucially, when jamming overlaps with pilot and data symbols in both time and frequency domains, it inflicts a severe bottleneck on receiver-side joint estimation and detection. Existing schemes often lack an effective framework to combat such jamming contamination, thereby failing to guarantee reliable transmission. To address this issue, we propose a Brownian bridge diffusion-assisted joint channel estimation and data detection (BBD-JCED) framework for jamming-resilient orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) receivers. The proposed framework consists of a jamming suppression module and a Brownian bridge-joint recovery module. The former identifies jamming-contaminated bins in the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain and suppresses the dominant jamming components through spectral notching. The latter establishes a Brownian bridge-based probabilistic graph to model the probabilistic transition process from the suppressed OFDM observation to the coded bits, and performs a reverse recovery process to enable enhanced joint channel estimation and data detection. Moreover, we derive a variational lower bound (VLB) to reformulate the intractable bit estimate problem into a tractable training objective, providing a probabilistic foundation for the loss function design. Furthermore, we develop a two-stage training algorithm to separately optimize the jamming suppression and Brownian bridge-joint recovery modules. Simulation results under representative jamming types demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior jamming suppression and bit recovery performance over the considered baseline schemes while maintaining competitive inference complexity.

items.title: A Geometric Coding Theorem
items.summary: arXiv:2607.13796v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper establishes a direct analogue of the classical Coding Theorem in the setting of symmetry groups. We consider computable bijections on the set of binary strings and define the symmetry prior of a string x as the probability that a randomly chosen symmetry from a given group G has x as its unique fixed point. We show that for any fix-retractable symmetry group G, a group admitting a computable section that selects an isolating symmetry for every string, the symmetry prior is a universal lower semi-computable semi-measure. In this case, the Geometric Coding Theorem holds. This result is a coding-theoretic restatement of a theorem of Trejo, Kreinovich and Longpr\'e, who showed that the complexity of describing a string by a symmetry with that string as its unique fixed point equals its Kolmogorov complexity. Our contribution is to recast it in terms of algorithmic probability and to treat the symmetry group as a parameter, identifying fix-retractability as exactly the condition under which symmetry complexity collapses onto Kolmogorov complexity.
